transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
Ukrainians gathered in San Francisco Sunday to protest the Trump administration's plan
to purchase diesel from Russia from member station KQED Christopher Allum reports.
Some demonstrators were crying, others held portraits of loved ones killed in the war.
They said President Trump's plan to buy over a million barrels of oil from Russia,
violates sanctions he signed into law last month, and is a betrayal of Ukrainians.
Nick Billigorsky is a Bay Area resident born in eastern Ukraine.
He says it's a political move that won't pay off.
One is it's immoral.
Two, it's illegal.
If it goes against the laws, it will be challenged.
And three, it's too small to make any sense, so it's just a terrible deal all around.
Demonstrators said they are writing to representatives in Congress to demand they enforce the sanctions.
For NPR News, I'm Christopher Allum in San Francisco.
Many leaders of Native American tribal nations are raising concerns about the Trump administration's
proposal for unprecedented changes to the next U.S. census.
It would reshape voting maps and how federal funding is distributed across the United States.
And Pierre's Hansi Lo Wang reports.
One proposed change is not to use the 2030 census to produce statistics about race and
ethnicity.
The topic has been part of the U.S. headcount since the first one in 1790.
Trump officials say they see a "reduced need" for that information, which is used for redistricting
and enforcing civil rights laws.
Megan Bishop of the National Congress of American Indians is an enrolled citizen of the native
village of Afognac in Alaska.
There's a significant concern about how federal funding would be distributed through grants
and other programs to tribes if that race-ethnicity census question is erased.
The public can comment on their proposal through November 2nd.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
The U.S. is now in the midst of the biggest and deadliest measles epidemic in decades.
With cases reported across the country, infectious disease experts say some vaccinated adults
should consider another measles shot.
NPR's Maria Godoy has more on our story.
Before vaccines, measles used to kill four to five hundred people in the U.S. each year.
Two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is 97 percent effective.
Most people vaccinated before 1989 probably received just one dose instead of the two
doses recommended for children today.
Dr. Larry Kousiolek of Northwestern University says traditionally, one dose has been considered
sufficient protection for adults not at high risk, but he says these days, "If you are
living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults
to go ahead and get that second dose."
If you're not sure of your vaccination history, he says there's no harm in getting an extra
dose of the MMR vaccine.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
In Asia, stocks closed down in part because of AI concerns.
South Korea's KOSPI dropped 3.65 percent, hitting its lowest level since late August.
This is NPR News.
For the fourth time in five days, the international airport in Saudi Arabia has been hit by projectiles.
Officials say the latest attack hit a passenger terminal and caused some injuries.
It was the same terminal hit on Saturday.
At least 12 people died in that attack, and more than 300 others were injured.
Saudis say the Houthi rebels in Yemen are responsible for the attacks.
Pakistan has imposed emergency rule in the province run by the political party of imprisoned
prime minister Imran Khan.
As Betsy Jules reports from Islamabad, this comes a week after Khan's party began a long
march toward the capital.
The move effectively suspends the provincial government, controlled by Khan's party, Pakistan,
Tariq and Saaf.
It hands some of those powers over to the federal government, which is run by two dynastic
political rivals of PTI and heavily influenced by the military.
It risks igniting significant political unrest.
The decision comes after talks between PTI and the federal government failed to halt
the march that has seen Khan supporters demanding his release.
The government says PTI's indifference about fighting terrorism in this border region with
Afghanistan justifies emergency rule.
For NPR News, I'm Betsy Jules in Islamabad.
Georgia is the new number one in college football this weekend.
After slipping past Alabama on Saturday 20-17, Notre Dame moved up to number two, followed
by Miami, Ohio State and defending champion Indiana.
Alabama stayed in sixth despite its loss, while Texas, who lost to an unranked Oklahoma
27-24 in the Red River rivalry, fell to seventh.
BYU, Mississippi and Texas Tech round out the top ten.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

topics.text: Ukrainians in San Francisco protest Trump administration plan to buy Russian diesel
Native American tribal leaders raise concerns over Trump proposal to drop race and ethnicity from 2030 census
U.S. measles epidemic prompts experts to suggest second MMR dose for some vaccinated adults
Asian stocks fall, with South Korea's KOSPI dropping 3.65 percent on AI concerns
Saudi Arabia's international airport hit by projectiles for fourth time in five days
Pakistan imposes emergency rule in Imran Khan's party-run province amid march on capital
Notre Dame rises to number two in college football after beating Alabama; Georgia takes top spot
